pages.title: About Slate and Sonal Systems
pages.description: Slate is a calorie journal for iPhone, built for Indian food by Sonal Systems Private Limited in Vadodara, Gujarat. Who makes it and how to reach us.
pages.lede: Slate is a calorie journal for iPhone, built for Indian food by Sonal Systems Private Limited, a company in Vadodara, Gujarat. You type what you ate the way you'd say it, and Slate puts a number next to it.

content: Slate is made by Sonal Systems Private Limited, founded in 2026 by Nirmal Amin and Nehal Amin. Nirmal writes the articles on this site.
Sonal Systems Private Limited is registered in India (CIN U62099GJ2026PTC179785). The office is at A-3, Mehsana Nagar, Nizampura, Vadodara 390002, Gujarat.

ul: Calories come from home recipes in grams and the Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT 2017). [How Slate counts calories](/how-slate-counts/) shows the arithmetic.
AI only reads lines Slate doesn't recognise, spots dishes in photos and powers chat. It never produces a calorie number, and your Slate isn't used to train AI models.
There's no login, and your data is stored in Mumbai, India. The [privacy policy](/privacy/) has the details.
Slate is free forever. Slate Plus is optional, at ₹399 a month or ₹2,999 a year.
Slate is not medical advice, and it's for people 18 or older.

body.h2: How do I reach the people behind Slate?
content: Write to [support@writeonslate.com](mailto:support@writeonslate.com) for help, feedback or questions about your data. [Support](/support/) answers the common questions.

pages.title: How Slate counts calories in Indian food
pages.description: How every number on Slate is worked out: home recipes in grams, IFCT 2017 values, cooked weights, katori sizes, outside food, rounding and cross-checks.
pages.lede: Every number on Slate starts from a home recipe in grams. Each ingredient's calories, protein, carbs and fat come from the Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT 2017), and the dish is then divided into the portions people eat: a katori, a roti, a plate.

body.h2: Where do the values come from?

ul: Energy for each ingredient is IFCT 2017's own value, converted from kilojoules at 4.184 kJ per calorie.
Pure fats such as oil and ghee have no energy value in the IFCT tables Slate uses, so they use IFCT's fat factor of 37 kJ per gram, about 8.84 calories per gram.
Ingredients IFCT doesn't list use USDA FoodData Central or the maker's label. Every dish page names the source for each ingredient.

body.h2: How does a recipe become a portion?
content: A dish is a home recipe written in raw grams, and adding up its ingredients gives the whole pot.

When a published cooked weight exists, the pot is divided by it to get calories per 100 g cooked, and a portion is its cooked weight. A katori is its volume in ml times the dish's density, so a 200 ml katori of thin dal weighs less than one of thick dal.
When there's no reliable cooked weight, a portion is a share of the recipe instead, such as one of four servings.
Calories are rounded to the nearest 5 and grams to the nearest whole number.

Restaurant and street versions usually use more oil, ghee or butter, and bigger servings. Slate shows them as a range: the fat in the recipe is multiplied up, the portion is scaled up, and anything extra a restaurant usually adds is counted on top. Each dish page shows the range and the reasons for it.

Each dish is compared with published figures, such as ICMR-NIN's food tables. When a credible source is more than 15% away from Slate's number, the dish page shows a range and explains the difference instead of a single number.

body.h2: Why do other sites show bigger numbers?
content: Many calorie sites list one serving without saying how big it is, often a large bowl or a restaurant recipe. Slate names the portion next to every number, so a 200 ml katori of home dal and a restaurant bowl don't get mixed up.

In the app you tell Slate the size of your katori and roti and how much oil you cook with, and it scales these numbers to your kitchen. AI only reads lines Slate doesn't recognise; it never produces a calorie number.
